rationale: B wins because it is tougher about reporter due diligence and less tempted by clever but unsupported inversion. Its line "A single average with no distribution behind it will not survive a data reporter's first question" is exactly the adult in the room. A has strong material, but "As Ramp customers, this beta group presumably already had spend visibility" is the kind of word that gets a pitch killed; if the premise is "presumably," it is not your headline. Slight margin because B still overreaches with "charging for the approval workflow."
gaps_in_A: "As Ramp customers, this beta group presumably already had spend visibility" is not grounded in the update. A flags the weakness, then still builds a headline on it.
"Ramp's new AI agent emails vendors to cancel" overstates the autonomy. The update says the agent drafts emails that finance approves.
"agent initiating a real-world business transaction" is too hot for the facts. Drafting an approval-gated email is not the same as initiating a transaction.
"An enterprise-AI reporter at a business-tech outlet" is better than "tech journalist," but still a little broad. The stronger beat is finance ops, procurement workflow, or SaaS pricing.
gaps_in_B: "Ramp's new agent cancels your software subscriptions" is wrong as written. The agent flags waste and drafts cancellation or renegotiation emails; finance approves them.
"Ramp is giving away the software-audit feature — and charging for the approval workflow" states a pricing model the update does not actually confirm.
"The beta figure is being published for the first time with today's launch" is an invented timing detail. Plausible is not the same as sourced.

"at the scale of $80B in annualized purchase volume" risks laundering total purchase volume into software-spend reach. B correctly asks for the split later, but the angle still leans on the big shiny number.
